blocks.text:
A single container started with `docker run` is easy to reason about. A production service is different: it needs several identical copies for capacity and availability, replacement of copies that crash, a way to roll out a new version without downtime, a stable address that survives restarts, secrets and configuration injected at start, and placement decisions across many machines. Doing this with shell scripts and one Docker host per application does not scale beyond a handful of services. A **container orchestrator** is software that takes a description of the desired deployment and continuously works to make the machines match it.

**Kubernetes** (abbreviated K8s) is the dominant open-source orchestrator. It originated at Google, is maintained by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, and is offered as a managed service by every large cloud provider (for example Amazon EKS, which appears in the AWS chapters of this guide). The earlier Docker chapters describe how one image becomes one container; this Part describes how that image runs as many containers on many nodes, how it is updated safely, and how the cluster configuration itself is stored in Git.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Environment and verification No Kubernetes cluster, Helm, Argo CD or registry was available on the build machine (no network, no container networking). Every manifest in this Part was parsed with PyYAML (`yaml.safe_load_all`, success reported) and cross-checked by script for selector, label, port and Secret-key consistency, but none was applied to a cluster. Command output is labelled `typical output (not run on the build machine)`. Version facts: per kubernetes.io/releases, consulted October 2026, the supported minor versions are 1.37, 1.36, 1.35 and 1.34 (1.34 reaches end of life on 2026-10-27). API versions and defaults marked `per kubernetes.io` were read from the official documentation in October 2026; items marked `from memory, verify before use` were not confirmed.

The running example is the `orders-service` (Spring Boot 3, Java 21, port 8080, health endpoint `/actuator/health`, database `orders`, user `orders_app`) built into the image `orders-service` in the Docker and CI chapters. The Spring Boot guide covers actuator and graceful shutdown in application terms; this Part covers the cluster side.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The declarative model

Kubernetes is operated by declaring **desired state** in objects and letting controllers reconcile reality towards it. An object is a record stored in the cluster, written as YAML with four top-level fields:

- `apiVersion` and `kind` identify the API group and resource type, for example `apps/v1` and `Deployment`.
- `metadata` holds the `name`, the `namespace`, `labels` and `annotations`.
- `spec` is the desired state, written by the user.
- `status` is the observed state, written by the cluster. A user never edits it.

The commands that matter are declarative: `kubectl apply -f file.yaml` stores the object, and the cluster then does whatever is needed. Imperative commands such as `kubectl scale` exist but leave no record in Git, which becomes a problem discussed later in the GitOps chapter.

#### Components

A cluster has a **control plane** (the decision makers) and **worker nodes** (the machines that run containers).

blocks.text:
#### The reconciliation loop

Every controller implements the same pattern: read the desired state, observe the actual state, compute the difference, act, and repeat. The loop is **level-triggered**: it compares states rather than reacting to individual events, so a missed event is corrected on the next pass. This is why Kubernetes recovers from crashes without special handling: a crashed Pod is simply a difference between `replicas: 3` and two ready Pods.

blocks.text:
#### Namespaces, contexts and clusters

A **namespace** partitions names and policies inside a cluster (for example `orders`, `payments`, `monitoring`). A **context** in the local kubeconfig file (`~/.kube/config`) combines a cluster, a user and a default namespace. Most operational accidents with `kubectl` come from running a correct command against the wrong context or namespace.

### Worked example

The commands below create a namespace, apply a Deployment and inspect the result. The cluster is assumed to be a local kind cluster.

blocks.code:
$ kubectl config current-context
kind-orders-lab
$ kubectl create namespace orders
namespace/orders created
$ kubectl apply -f 30-deployment.yaml
deployment.apps/orders-service created
$ kubectl get deployment,replicaset,pods -n orders
NAME                             READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
deployment.apps/orders-service   3/3     3            3           48s

NAME                                        DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
replicaset.apps/orders-service-6d8f7b9c5d   3         3         3       48s

NAME                                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/orders-service-6d8f7b9c5d-4kq7x   1/1     Running   0          48s
pod/orders-service-6d8f7b9c5d-9xw2p   1/1     Running   0          48s
pod/orders-service-6d8f7b9c5d-mt5zr   1/1     Running   0          48s

blocks.text:
What to notice: the Deployment owns a ReplicaSet whose name carries a hash of the Pod template, and the ReplicaSet owns the Pods; each Pod name is the ReplicaSet name plus a random suffix. Changing the Pod template (for example the image tag) produces a new ReplicaSet with a new hash, which is how a rollout is represented.

To observe the reconciliation loop directly, delete one Pod and list again; the ReplicaSet creates a replacement within seconds.

blocks.code:
$ kubectl delete pod orders-service-6d8f7b9c5d-4kq7x -n orders
pod "orders-service-6d8f7b9c5d-4kq7x" deleted
$ kubectl get pods -n orders
NAME                              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
orders-service-6d8f7b9c5d-9xw2p   1/1     Running   0          2m
orders-service-6d8f7b9c5d-mt5zr   1/1     Running   0          2m

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

This exercise requires a local cluster; it was not run on the build machine. kind (Kubernetes in Docker) and minikube are the two common choices; both run a cluster inside containers or a VM on the developer machine and both need a working Docker installation and internet access to pull images.

1. Install `kubectl` and `kind`, then create the cluster with `kind create cluster --name orders-lab`.
2. Run `kubectl cluster-info` and `kubectl get nodes` and record the node name and the Kubernetes version.
3. Run `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` and match each Pod to a component in the table above (the API server, etcd, scheduler and controller manager run as Pods on a kind control-plane node).
4. Apply a Deployment of three replicas of any public image, delete one Pod, and observe the replacement.
5. Run `kubectl get events -n default --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp` and trace the events (Scheduled, Pulling, Pulled, Created, Started) to the sequence diagram above.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: a command was run against the wrong cluster

**Scenario.** A developer tests a change to the `orders-service` Deployment on a local cluster, switches terminals, and runs `kubectl delete deployment orders-service -n orders`.

**Symptoms.** The local cluster shows nothing changed; the production dashboards show the orders-service Pods terminating.

**Diagnosis.** `kubectl config current-context` in the terminal that ran the command prints the production context. Shell history confirms the order of commands. **Root cause.** The kubeconfig has a single `current-context` that is shared by every terminal using that file. Switching context in one terminal changes it for all of them.

**Fix.** Re-apply the Deployment from Git (`kubectl apply -f` or a GitOps sync) and verify with `kubectl rollout status` `deployment/orders-service -n orders`.

**Prevention.** Show the context in the shell prompt, use a separate kubeconfig file per environment selected with `KUBECONFIG`, give developers read-only roles in production, and prefer deployment through the pipeline over human `kubectl` access. Production changes made only through GitOps make this class of accident recoverable in minutes.

#### Problem: kubectl shows no resources although the application is running

**Scenario.** `kubectl get pods` returns `No resources found in default namespace.` while the service is serving traffic.

**Symptoms.** An empty list, and a colleague sees the Pods with the same command.

**Diagnosis.** `kubectl config view --minify --output 'jsonpath={..namespace}'` prints an empty value (the `default` namespace). `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces` lists the Pods in `orders`.

**Root cause.** Resources are namespaced, and the context has no default namespace set.

**Fix.** Pass `-n orders` explicitly, or set it once with `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=orders`.

**Prevention.** Always write `-n <namespace>` in scripts and documentation, and put `namespace:` in every manifest (as the manifests in this Part do) so that `kubectl apply` is unambiguous.

### Questions to expect

#### What problem does Kubernetes solve that Docker alone does not?

Docker runs containers on one host. Kubernetes schedules containers across many nodes, restarts failed ones, scales the number of copies, rolls out new versions gradually, provides stable service discovery and load balancing, and injects configuration and secrets, all from a declarative description.

#### Name the control plane components and the role of each.

The API server is the only entry point and the only writer to etcd. etcd stores the cluster state. The scheduler assigns unscheduled Pods to nodes. The controller manager runs the reconciliation loops (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job and others). On each node the kubelet runs the Pods and kube-proxy implements Service networking.

#### What is a reconciliation loop, and why is it called level-triggered?

A controller repeatedly compares desired state (`spec`) with observed state (`status`) and acts on the difference. It is level-triggered because it reacts to the current difference rather than to a particular event, so a lost event or a restarted controller does not leave the system permanently wrong.

#### What happens between kubectl apply of a Deployment and a running container?

The API server validates and stores the Deployment. The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pod objects without a node. The scheduler binds each Pod to a node. The kubelet of that node sees the binding, pulls the image through the runtime, starts the containers and reports status.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Kubernetes continuously reconciles actual state towards declared state; spec is written by users, status by the cluster.
- The API server is the single gateway to etcd; the scheduler, controllers and kubelets all work through it.
- A Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pods; a Pod template change creates a new ReplicaSet.
- Context and namespace mistakes cause real outages; make both visible and explicit.
- Local clusters (kind, minikube) are for learning and testing; managed services run production control planes.

sections.title: Core Objects: Pods, Deployments, Services and Configuration

blocks.text:
### Configuration

Kubernetes has dozens of resource types, but a typical backend service uses a small set: a Deployment to run copies, a Service to give them one address, an Ingress to expose them outside the cluster, and a ConfigMap and Secret to supply settings. This chapter defines each object, shows its manifest and states the mistakes that waste the most time.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Pod

A **Pod** is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP address, communication over `localhost`), can share volumes, and are always scheduled onto the same node together. Most Pods contain one application container; additional containers (sidecars) support it, for example a log shipper. Pods are ephemeral: each replacement Pod has a new name and a new IP address. The Pod phases are Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown (per kubernetes.io).

The `restartPolicy` field (per kubernetes.io: `Always`, `OnFailure` or `Never`, default `Always`) controls whether the kubelet restarts a container that exits. When a container keeps failing, the kubelet restarts it with an exponential backoff delay of 10 s, 20 s, 40 s and so on, capped at 300 s (five minutes), and resets the timer after the container has run ten minutes without problems (per kubernetes.io). The Pod status `CrashLoopBackOff` is the visible symptom of this delay.

#### ReplicaSet and Deployment

A **ReplicaSet** keeps a specified number of identical Pods running, selected by labels. A **Deployment** manages ReplicaSets to provide declarative updates: changing the Pod template creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts replicas from the old one to the new one according to the update strategy. Deployments are the standard object for stateless services such as the `orders-service`. The API version is `apps/v1` (per kubernetes.io).

The default strategy is `RollingUpdate`. Its two parameters bound the transition (per kubernetes.io):

- `maxUnavailable`: how many Pods below the desired count are tolerated during the update; default 25 percent. It cannot be 0 if `maxSurge` is 0.
- `maxSurge`: how many Pods above the desired count may exist during the update; default 25 percent, rounded up when expressed as a percentage.

Related defaults (per kubernetes.io): `progressDeadlineSeconds` is 600 and the Deployment keeps 10 old ReplicaSets (`revisionHistoryLimit`) for rollback. The `orders-service` manifest sets `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0`, which never reduces capacity: a new Pod must become Ready before an old one is stopped.

blocks.text:
#### Labels and selectors

**Labels** are key-value pairs on objects (`app: orders-service`). **Selectors** choose objects by label. Selectors are the only coupling mechanism: a Deployment selects its Pods, a Service selects the Pods that receive traffic, a PodDisruptionBudget selects the Pods it protects. A selector that does not match the labels in the Pod template silently selects nothing; the API server rejects the case of a Deployment whose own selector does not match its template, but it does not check a Service selector at all.

#### Service

A **Service** gives a set of Pods one stable virtual IP and DNS name. Pods come and go; the Service name does not. The control plane tracks the Ready Pods that match the selector (stored as EndpointSlice objects; from memory, verify before use), and kube-proxy on every node programs rules that distribute connections across them. Inside the cluster a Service is reachable as `orders-service` from the same namespace and as `orders-service.orders.svc` from another namespace.

rows: Exposes the Service on a cluster-internal IP; reachable only from within the cluster. The default.
Exposes the Service on each node's IP at a static port; the control plane allocates it from a range (default 30000-32767).
Exposes the Service externally using an external load balancer provided by the cloud.
Maps the Service to a DNS name in the `externalName` field; no proxying.

blocks.text:
#### Ingress and the Gateway API

A Service of type LoadBalancer creates one cloud load balancer per Service, which is expensive for many services. An **Ingress** (`networking.k8s.io/v1`, per kubernetes.io) is a set of HTTP routing rules (host and path to Service) implemented by an **ingress controller** such as ingress-nginx, which must be installed separately; the object does nothing without it. Per kubernetes.io the Kubernetes project recommends the **Gateway API** instead of Ingress, and the Ingress API is frozen: it receives no further changes. The Gateway API uses `Gateway` and `HTTPRoute` objects (group `gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`; from memory, verify before use) and supports weighted traffic splitting, which the canary section in the deployment strategies chapter uses. Existing Ingress resources continue to work.

#### ConfigMap and Secret

A **ConfigMap** holds non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs or files. A **Secret** holds sensitive values. Both are injected into containers as environment variables (`envFrom`, `env.valueFrom`) or as mounted files. Spring Boot reads environment variables by relaxed binding, so `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` sets `spring.datasource.url` without any change to `application.properties`.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: A Secret is not encrypted by default. Per kubernetes.io, Secrets are by default stored unencrypted in the API server's underlying data store (etcd); anyone with API access, or with access to etcd, can retrieve them. The values in a manifest or in `kubectl get secret -o yaml` are base64 encoded, which per the documentation obscures them but does not provide any useful level of confidentiality. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, and `echo cGFzc3dvcmQ= | base64 -d` reveals the value. Mitigations: enable encryption at rest for etcd, restrict access with RBAC, keep Secret manifests out of Git, and consider an external secret store (see the secrets chapter in the pipeline security material).

#### Namespace, Job, CronJob

A **Job** (`batch/v1`, per kubernetes.io) runs Pods to completion. A **CronJob** creates Jobs on a schedule (`batch/v1`; from memory, verify before use), with `concurrencyPolicy` set to `Allow`, `Forbid` or `Replace` and history limits for finished Jobs. These suit the nightly archive task in the manifest set later in this Part.

### Worked example

The manifests below describe the namespace, configuration and Secret for the `orders-service`. The file layout matches the complete manifest set in the next chapter.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: orders
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: orders-platform
blocks.title: 00-namespace.yaml (validated with PyYAML, not applied to a cluster)

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: orders-config
  namespace: orders
data:
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://orders-db:5432/orders
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: orders_app
  SERVER_SHUTDOWN: graceful
  SPRING_LIFECYCLE_TIMEOUT_PER_SHUTDOWN_PHASE: 25s
  MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINT_HEALTH_PROBES_ENABLED: "true"
  JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: orders-db-secret
  namespace: orders
type: Opaque
stringData:
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD: change-me-before-use
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: change-me-before-use
blocks.title: 10-config.yaml (validated with PyYAML, not applied to a cluster)

blocks.text:
What to notice: `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` addresses the database by the Service name `orders-db`, which resolves through cluster DNS; `SERVER_SHUTDOWN` and `SPRING_LIFECYCLE_TIMEOUT_PER_SHUTDOWN_PHASE` map to `server.shutdown` and `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase`; and the password is in the Secret, not in the ConfigMap. The placeholder password text is deliberately not a usable credential, and the file must not be committed with a real value (see the problems below and the GitOps chapter).

The Service and Ingress that expose the Deployment follow.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-service
  namespace: orders
  labels:
    app: orders-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: orders-service
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: orders-service
  namespace: orders
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: orders.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-service
                port:
                  name: http
blocks.title: 40-service-ingress.yaml (validated with PyYAML, not applied to a cluster)

blocks.text: The Service forwards port 80 to the container port named `http` (8080). Referring to the port by name means the Service keeps working if the container port number changes. `ingressClassName: nginx` assumes that ingress-nginx is installed (an assumption of this example), and `orders.example.com` is a reserved example domain.

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

This exercise requires a cluster and was not run on the build machine.

1. Apply the namespace, ConfigMap and Secret, then run `kubectl get configmap orders-config -n orders -o` `yaml`.
2. Run `kubectl get secret orders-db-secret -n orders -o jsonpath='{.data.SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD}'` `| base64 -d` and confirm that the plain-text value is recovered in one command.
3. Apply the Deployment and Service from the next chapter, then edit the Service selector to `app: orders-servise` (a deliberate typo) and apply it again.
4. Run `kubectl get endpointslices -n orders` and observe that the Service has no endpoints. Correct the selector and observe the endpoints return.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: Service has no endpoints

**Scenario.** After a release that renamed a label, requests through the `orders-service` Service time out, although all Pods show `1/1 Running`.

**Symptoms.** Connection timeouts or refused connections via the Service name; direct requests to a Pod IP succeed. The Ingress returns 503.

**Diagnosis.** `kubectl get endpointslices -n orders` shows an empty ENDPOINTS column. `kubectl describe` `service orders-service -n orders` prints `Endpoints: <none>`. Comparing `kubectl get service orders-service -n` `orders -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'` with `kubectl get pods -n orders --show-labels` reveals the mismatch. **Root cause.** The Service selector (`app: orders-service`) no longer matches the labels in the Pod template. A second cause with the same symptom is a Pod that is Running but not Ready, because only Ready Pods are endpoints.

**Fix.** Make the selector and template labels identical, or fix the failing readiness probe.

**Prevention.** Keep selector labels stable and minimal (`app`), never change them in a release, put varying data such as `version` in labels that no selector uses, and add a post-deploy check that `kubectl get endpointslices` is non-empty.

#### Problem: ImagePullBackOff

**Scenario.** A new release `orders-service:1.4.1` is applied; the new Pods never start while the old Pods keep serving.

**Symptoms.** `kubectl get pods` shows `ErrImagePull` and then `ImagePullBackOff`. The rollout stalls and after `progressDeadlineSeconds` the Deployment condition reports `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.

**Diagnosis.** `kubectl describe pod <pod> -n orders` lists in Events a message such as `Failed to pull image ...` `not found` or `unauthorized`.

**Root cause.** One of three causes: the tag does not exist in the registry (the CI push failed or used a different tag), the name or registry host is misspelled, or the cluster has no credentials for a private registry (no `imagePullSecrets`, or the node role lacks permission on the registry).

**Fix.** Correct the tag or name, or create a registry Secret with `kubectl create secret docker-registry` and reference it under `imagePullSecrets`. The old Pods remained available because `maxUnavailable: 0` held the rollout; `kubectl` `rollout undo deployment/orders-service -n orders` returns to the previous ReplicaSet if needed.

**Prevention.** Deploy only an image reference that the pipeline has just pushed and verified, pin to an immutable tag or digest, and let the pipeline wait for `kubectl rollout status` so that a stalled rollout fails the job.

### Questions to expect

#### What is a Pod and why do containers in a Pod share an IP address?

A Pod is a group of one or more containers scheduled together that share a network namespace and optionally volumes. Sharing the namespace gives them one IP and lets them communicate over `localhost`, which suits tightly coupled helpers such as a sidecar.

#### What is the relationship between Deployment, ReplicaSet and Pod?

A Deployment owns ReplicaSets, one per Pod template revision. A ReplicaSet keeps the desired number of Pods of its template running. During an update the Deployment controller scales the new ReplicaSet up and the old one down.

#### Explain maxSurge and maxUnavailable.

They bound a rolling update. `maxSurge` is the number of extra Pods allowed above the desired count; `maxUnavailable` is the number of Pods allowed to be unavailable. Both default to 25 percent. With `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0` capacity never drops, at the cost of needing room for one extra Pod.

#### How does a Service find its Pods?

By a label selector. The control plane keeps the list of Ready matching Pods and kube-proxy routes connections to them. A Pod that is not Ready is removed from the list.

#### Compare ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer.

ClusterIP is reachable only inside the cluster. NodePort adds a static port on every node. LoadBalancer adds a cloud load balancer in front of the NodePorts. Each type builds on the previous one.

#### Are Kubernetes Secrets secure?

By default they are only base64 encoded and stored unencrypted in etcd. They need encryption at rest, RBAC, and ideally an external secret manager. Committing a Secret manifest to Git exposes the value to everyone with repository access.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Pods are ephemeral; Deployments keep the desired number of them and perform rolling updates through ReplicaSets.
- Selectors connect everything; a wrong label produces a Service with no endpoints and no error message.
- Rolling update defaults are 25 percent surge and 25 percent unavailable; the orders-service uses surge 1 and unavailable 0.
- Secrets are base64 encoded, not encrypted; treat the manifest as sensitive and keep it out of Git.
- Ingress is frozen; Gateway API is the recommended direction.

Shipping a new version of a service is the most common cause of production incidents. The Deployment object in the previous chapters performs one specific strategy (a rolling update); the choice of strategy decides how many users meet a defective release, how long they meet it, and how quickly it can be withdrawn. This chapter defines the standard strategies, shows how each is expressed in Kubernetes, and quantifies the difference with a simulation. It then treats the two problems that strategies alone cannot solve: database schema changes that must work with two application versions at once, and the separation of deployment from release with feature flags.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Deployment and release are different events

A **deployment** puts a new version of the code on infrastructure. A **release** exposes its behaviour to users. For simple changes they coincide. Treating them as separate events is the basis of every strategy below: code can be deployed and verified before any user reaches it, and exposure can be increased gradually and withdrawn quickly.

#### The strategies

rows: Stop all old Pods, then start new Pods
Replace Pods gradually; both versions serve traffic
Defect reaches a growing share before detection
Run a full second environment; switch all traffic at once
All users hit a defect at the switch
Send a small, growing share of traffic to the new version
Needs good metrics and a routing layer
Mirror real traffic to the new version; discard its responses
Side effects of the duplicate requests
Split users by rule to compare a business metric

blocks.text:
*Deployment strategies compared. Rollback speeds are typical orders of magnitude, not measurements.*

#### Recreate and rolling

`strategy.type: Recreate` terminates every old Pod before creating new ones, which causes an outage but guarantees that two versions never run together; it is appropriate for a singleton that cannot tolerate two instances. The `RollingUpdate` default (parameters in the core objects chapter) keeps the service up but means that **two versions** **run side by side** for the length of the rollout. Everything that is shared (the database, the message format, cached data, the API contract) must therefore work with both versions. A rolling update also has no notion of error rate: Kubernetes advances as long as new Pods pass their readiness probe, so a release that starts correctly and fails on every second request completes the rollout.

blocks.text:
#### Blue-green

Two complete environments exist: **blue** (current) and **green** (new). Green is deployed and tested without user traffic, for example through a separate preview Service. The release is a single switch of the router from blue to green. Rollback is the reverse switch, which takes seconds because blue is still running. In Kubernetes the simplest form uses two Deployments that differ by a label `track: blue` and `track: green`, and a Service whose selector names the live track:

blocks.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-service
  namespace: orders
spec:
  selector:
    app: orders-service
    track: green
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80

blocks.text:
The costs: double capacity during the release, and the switch exposes all users at once. Blue-green gives fast rollback and testing before exposure; it does not by itself limit the number of users affected by a defect that tests missed.

#### Canary

A **canary release** sends a small share of real traffic (for example 5 percent) to the new version while the rest stays on the old one, compares metrics of both, and increases the share in steps only while the comparison is healthy. The name refers to the canary in a coal mine. Two requirements make it work: a routing layer that can split traffic by weight (a Gateway API `HTTPRoute`, a service mesh, an ingress with canary support) and an automated judgement of health. Without the second, a canary is only a slower manual rollout.

blocks.code:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: orders-canary
  namespace: orders
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public-gateway
  hostnames: ["orders.example.com"]
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: orders-service-stable
          port: 80
          weight: 95
        - name: orders-service-canary
          port: 80
          weight: 5
blocks.title: gateway-httproute.yaml (illustrative configuration, validated with PyYAML, not run)

blocks.text: The `HTTPRoute` splits 95 to 5 between two Services; this assumes a Gateway named `public-gateway` and a Gateway API implementation in the cluster, and the field names are `from memory, verify before use`. Changing the two weights is a Git change. **Progressive delivery** controllers automate the stepping and the analysis: Argo Rollouts replaces the Deployment with a `Rollout` object that lists steps, and Flagger drives a canary from metrics (both `from` `memory, verify before use`; neither was installed on the build machine).

blocks.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: orders-service
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 10
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-service
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5
        - pause: {duration: 2m}
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: {duration: 2m}
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: {duration: 2m}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: orders-service
          image: ghcr.io/example/orders-service:1.4.1
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
blocks.title: rollout.yaml (illustrative configuration, validated with PyYAML, not run)

blocks.text: The steps raise the weight to 5, 25 and 50 percent with a two-minute pause each; a full configuration adds an analysis template that queries the metrics store and aborts the rollout automatically if the error rate or latency exceeds a threshold. Without a traffic router the Rollout approximates the weight by the ratio of Pod counts (from memory, verify before use), which is coarse for few replicas.

blocks.text:
#### Shadow and A/B

In a **shadow** (dark launch) the router copies real requests to the new version and discards its responses; users see only the old version's answers. This tests performance and correctness under real traffic with no user impact, but the new version must not perform side effects such as charging a card or sending an email twice, so it needs stubs or a separate database. An **A/B test** splits users by a stable rule (header, cookie, user id) to compare a business metric such as conversion; it is an experiment technique and not a safety mechanism, although the same routing layer implements it.

blocks.text:
#### Feature flags

A **feature flag** is a runtime switch in the code (`if (flags.enabled("new_checkout", user))`). The new code path ships in an ordinary deployment with the flag off; the release is then a configuration change, in steps, for chosen users or a percentage; the rollback is turning the flag off, without a deployment. Flags decouple the two events at the finest granularity and are the standard companion to trunk-based development. The costs are real: every flag doubles the code paths to test, stale flags become dead code and confusing conditions, and a flag service becomes a dependency. Remove each flag after the release is complete.

#### Rollback procedures

A rollback is only as fast as the mechanism that was prepared before the release:

rows: git revert COMMIT, merge, controller syncs
Set the weight to 0 or abort the Rollout
blocks.caption: Rollback mechanisms.

blocks.text:
A rollback of the application does not roll back the database. That is the subject of the next section.

### Database migrations during a rollout

During a rolling update, a canary or a blue-green preview, **two application versions use one database at the** **same time**. Spring Boot applications commonly manage the schema with **Flyway** or **Liquibase**: versioned migration scripts (for Flyway `src/main/resources/db/migration/V12__add_order_state.sql`) run at application startup, in order, and are recorded in a history table. Flyway takes a database lock so that concurrent starters do not apply the same script twice (from memory, verify before use). If a script renames or drops something that the old version still reads, the old Pods fail the moment the first new Pod runs the migration, and a rollback of the application cannot repair it.

The **expand-contract** pattern (also called parallel change) splits a breaking schema change into backward-compatible releases:

1. **Expand.** Add the new structure without removing the old (a new nullable column, a new table). Both versions work. Backfill existing rows.
2. **Migrate.** Deploy the version that writes both structures and reads the new one. Backfill rows written by the old version meanwhile.
3. **Contract.** After no old version remains and rollback to it is no longer needed, a later release removes the old structure.

blocks.text: The demonstration below applies the pattern to a table `orders`. SQLite stands in for PostgreSQL because no PostgreSQL cluster was started for this chapter; the two statements that matter (`ADD COLUMN`, `RENAME COLUMN`) exist in both, but the transactional and locking behaviour differs, so the output shows the logic and not the production behaviour. The code and its real output:

blocks.code:
"""Expand-contract demonstration. SQLite stands in for PostgreSQL (similar DDL)."""
import sqlite3

def v1_app(db):      # old release: knows only column "status"
    db.execute("INSERT INTO orders(id, status) VALUES (?, 'NEW')", (v1_app.n,)); v1_app.n += 1
    return db.execute("SELECT status FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1").fetchone()[0]
v1_app.n = 100

def v2_app(db):      # new release: writes both columns during the transition, reads the new one
    db.execute("INSERT INTO orders(id, status, order_state) VALUES (?, 'NEW', 'NEW')",
               (v2_app.n,))
    v2_app.n += 1
    return db.execute("SELECT order_state FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1").fetchone()[0]
v2_app.n = 200

def attempt(label, fn, db):
    try:
        print("  %-26s -> %s" % (label, fn(db)))
    except sqlite3.Error as e:
        print("  %-26s -> ERROR: %s" % (label, e))

print("A. Naive single-step migration: rename the column during the rollout")
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT NOT NULL)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'PAID')")
db.execute("ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN status TO order_state")
attempt("old release (v1) still running", v1_app, db)

print("B. Expand-contract")
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT NOT NULL)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'PAID')")
print(" step 1 expand: add nullable column, backfill")
db.execute("ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN order_state TEXT")
db.execute("UPDATE orders SET order_state = status WHERE order_state IS NULL")
attempt("old release (v1) running", v1_app, db)
attempt("new release (v2) running", v2_app, db)
print(" step 2 migrate: all pods run v2; backfill rows written by v1 meanwhile")
db.execute("UPDATE orders SET order_state = status WHERE order_state IS NULL")
missing = db.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE order_state IS NULL").fetchone()[0]
print("  rows without order_state:", missing)
print(" step 3 contract (a later release): drop the old column")
db.execute("ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN status")
print("  columns now:", [r[1] for r in db.execute("PRAGMA table_info(orders)")])

blocks.text:
Practical rules for PostgreSQL migrations:

- Add columns as nullable or with a constant default; add `NOT NULL` only in a later release after the backfill is complete.
- Backfill large tables in batches outside the migration transaction, to avoid long locks.
- Create indexes with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, which cannot run inside a transaction, so Flyway needs that script configured to run without one (from memory, verify before use).
- Never edit an applied migration; Flyway validates checksums and refuses to start.
- Run migrations in a separate step before the rollout (a Kubernetes Job or a pipeline stage) when they are slow, so that application Pods do not fail their startup probe while a migration holds the lock.

**Backward-compatible API changes** follow the same logic for clients and for other services: add fields, never remove or rename them in the same release; accept unknown fields (tolerant reader); add new endpoints beside old ones; version the API when behaviour must change; remove an old element only after telemetry shows that nothing calls it.

### Zero-downtime deployment checklist

1. The Pod template has readiness, liveness and startup probes that reflect the application only (see the probes section of the resources chapter).
2. `maxUnavailable: 0` and `maxSurge` of at least 1 for rolling updates, with spare cluster capacity for the surge Pods.
3. A `preStop` delay, graceful shutdown enabled and a grace period longer than both.
4. A PodDisruptionBudget so that node drains do not remove too many Pods.
5. At least two replicas spread over nodes or zones.
6. Database changes follow expand-contract; the old and the new version are both compatible with the schema at every step.
7. API and message formats are backward compatible for at least one release.
8. The pipeline waits for `kubectl rollout status` and fails the job if the rollout does not complete within the deadline.
9. Error rate and latency are watched during and after the rollout, with an automatic or rehearsed rollback.
10. The rollback was tested in staging; the previous image is still in the registry.

### Worked example: simulating a bad release

No cluster was available, so the exposure of a defective release under three strategies was **simulated** in Python. The program models request counts, not real systems; the numbers below depend entirely on the stated assumptions and must not be read as measurements of Kubernetes or of any tool. Assumptions (all chosen for this exercise): 200 requests per second; the defective version fails 30 percent of its requests and the good version 0.1 percent; an alarm fires above a 5 percent error rate. Rolling and blue-green are judged by the **overall** error rate over a 60 s window and then wait 60 s for a human to start the rollback (the rollback of a rolling update takes 10 s per replaced Pod; blue-green switches back in 5 s). The canary is judged by an automated check of the **canary's own** error rate over 30 s with no human delay, and its rollback takes 10 s. Rolling replaces one of ten Pods every 20 s from t = 30 s; blue-green switches all traffic at t = 30 s; the canary steps through 5, 25, 50 and 100 percent every 120 s.

blocks.code:
"""Simulation (not a real cluster): exposure of a bad release under three strategies."""
import random

RPS = 200            # requests per second, constant (assumed)
BAD_ERR = 0.30       # fraction of requests failing on the bad version (assumed)
GOOD_ERR = 0.001     # background error rate of the good version (assumed)
ALARM = 0.05         # alert threshold on the error rate of a window (assumed)
WINDOW = 30          # seconds of data per evaluation (assumed)
HORIZON = 600        # simulated seconds


def run(name, new_share, metric, window, decision_delay, rollback_secs, seed=7):
    """metric 'global': error rate of all traffic over `window` s; 'version': error rate of the new
    version only (needs >= 100 requests).  The alarm fires when the rate exceeds ALARM;
    `decision_delay` s later the rollback starts and lasts rollback_secs(share) s."""
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    total = bad_failed = 0
    hist = []              # per second: (all_requests, all_errors, new_requests, new_errors)
    alarm = start_rb = back_at = None
    peak = 0.0
    for t in range(HORIZON):
        share = new_share(t)
        if start_rb is not None and t >= start_rb:
            share = share_at_rb * max(0.0, 1.0 - (t - start_rb) / float(rb_len))
            if t >= back_at:
                share = 0.0
        peak = max(peak, share)
        n_new = sum(1 for _ in range(RPS) if rnd.random() < share)
        e_new = sum(1 for _ in range(n_new) if rnd.random() < BAD_ERR)
        e_old = sum(1 for _ in range(RPS - n_new) if rnd.random() < GOOD_ERR)
        total += RPS
        bad_failed += e_new
        hist.append((RPS, e_new + e_old, n_new, e_new))
        if alarm is None and len(hist) >= window:
            w = hist[-window:]
            if metric == "global":
                rate = sum(x[1] for x in w) / float(sum(x[0] for x in w))
                ok = True
            else:
                nn = sum(x[2] for x in w)
                rate = sum(x[3] for x in w) / float(nn) if nn else 0.0
                ok = nn >= 100
            if ok and rate > ALARM:
                alarm = t
                start_rb = t + decision_delay
                share_at_rb = new_share(start_rb)
                rb_len = rollback_secs(share_at_rb)
                back_at = start_rb + rb_len
    return dict(name=name, total=total, failed=bad_failed, peak=peak * 100,
                alarm=alarm, back=back_at)


def rolling_share(t):          # 10 pods, one replaced every 20 s from t=30
    return 0.0 if t < 30 else min(1.0, (1 + (t - 30) // 20) / 10.0)


def bg_share(t):               # all traffic switched to green at t=30
    return 0.0 if t < 30 else 1.0


def canary_share(t):           # 5 % at 30 s, 25 % at 150 s, 50 % at 270 s, 100 % at 390 s
    if t < 30: return 0.0
    if t < 150: return 0.05
    if t < 270: return 0.25
    if t < 390: return 0.50
    return 1.0


runs = [
    run("rolling, manual rollback", rolling_share, "global", 60, 60,
        lambda sh: max(10, round(sh * 10) * 10)),
    run("blue-green, manual rollback", bg_share, "global", 60, 60, lambda sh: 5),
    run("canary, automated analysis", canary_share, "version", 30, 0, lambda sh: 10),
]
print("Assumptions: %d req/s, bad version fails %d %% of requests, alarm above %d %% error rate"
      % (RPS, BAD_ERR * 100, ALARM * 100))
print("rolling/blue-green: global 60 s window + 60 s human delay;")
print("canary: per-version 30 s window, no delay")
print("%-30s %8s %7s %8s %7s %9s"
      % ("strategy", "failed", "peak %", "alarm@s", "back@s", "of total"))
for r in runs:
    print("%-30s %8d %7.0f %8s %7s %8.2f%%"
          % (r["name"], r["failed"], r["peak"], r["alarm"], r["back"],
                                                 100.0 * r["failed"] / r["total"]))

blocks.text:
Reading the result carefully:

- **Exposure is set by detection time and by the share of traffic at that time.** Blue-green failed more requests than rolling because the same manual detection delay applied while 100 percent of traffic was on the defective version; rolling had reached 60 percent. Blue-green is not safer on exposure in this model; its advantage is the rollback speed (5 s against 120 s here).
- **A global threshold hides a small canary.** At a 5 percent share and a 30 percent failure rate the overall error rate is 0.05 x 0.30 = 1.5 percent, below the 5 percent alarm. The canary was caught only because the analysis compared the canary's own error rate. Comparing per version is essential.
- **Automation, not the percentage alone, produced most of the gain.** The canary alarm fired at 39 s and the rollback completed at 49 s; there was no 60 s human delay.
- Changing any assumption changes the numbers: a slower alarm, a lower failure rate or a different step schedule would shift all three results. The model has no latency, retries, caching or user stickiness.

### Hands-on

This exercise requires a cluster and was not run on the build machine.

1. Deploy the blue and green Deployments (copies of the `orders-service` Deployment with the label `track` and different image tags) and the Service above. Switch the selector with the `kubectl patch` command, then switch back, and time both operations.
2. Change the simulation parameters: set `ALARM` to 0.01 and `WINDOW` to 30, rerun, and describe how the three results change and why.
3. Write a Flyway migration pair for renaming `customer_name` to `customer_full_name` in three releases, following the expand-contract table above, and state which release may be rolled back at each stage.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: a bad release reached 100 percent of traffic

**Scenario.** Release 1.5.0 passed tests and was rolled out by the default rolling update. The new code fails on orders that contain a discount code.

**Symptoms.** Error rate rises gradually during the rollout from 0 to 15 percent; the alert fires after the rollout has finished, 12 minutes later.

**Diagnosis.** The dashboard shows errors starting at the first minute of the rollout, concentrated on the new Pods (the version label on the metric separates them). `kubectl rollout history` identifies the previous revision.

**Root cause.** The rolling update advances on readiness, not on business metrics, and no automated analysis or small canary stage existed; detection depended on a global alert with a long window.

**Fix.** `kubectl rollout undo deployment/orders-service -n orders`, then verify that the error rate returns to the baseline. **Prevention.** Add a canary stage with per-version analysis (Argo Rollouts or Flagger), label metrics with the application version, alert on version-specific error rate, put risky features behind flags, and rehearse the rollback.

#### Problem: a migration broke the old version during a rollout

**Scenario.** Release 1.6.0 renames the column `status` to `order_state` in the same Flyway script that the first new Pod runs at startup.

**Symptoms.** As soon as the first new Pod starts, the old Pods return 500 with `column "status" does not exist`; the rollout is aborted, but rolling back the application does not help.

**Diagnosis.** The old Pods log `PSQLException: ERROR: column "status" does not exist`. The Flyway history table shows the new version applied.

**Root cause.** A breaking schema change ran while the old version was still serving, and a rollback of the code cannot undo a schema change.

**Fix.** Restore the old column or add a compatibility column through a hot fix migration, then redeploy.

**Prevention.** Use expand-contract; test the previous application version against the migrated schema in the pipeline (run the old integration tests against the new schema); never combine a destructive change with the release that depends on it.

### Questions to expect

#### Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments.

Rolling replaces Pods gradually with little extra capacity but runs two versions together and detects nothing beyond readiness. Blue-green runs a full second environment and switches all traffic at once, with a seconds-fast rollback and double capacity. Canary exposes a small share first and increases it while metrics stay healthy, which limits the damage of a defect at the cost of a routing layer and automated analysis.

#### How is a database schema change made safe in a rolling update?

With expand-contract: add the new structure compatibly, deploy code that handles both, backfill, and remove the old structure in a later release. During the rollout old and new application versions must both work with the schema.

#### How does Kubernetes roll back a Deployment?

`kubectl rollout undo` scales the previous ReplicaSet back up and the current one down, using the revision history (10 revisions are kept by default, per kubernetes.io). In a GitOps setup the rollback is a Git revert.

#### Why can a canary at 5 percent miss a defective release?

If the alarm uses the overall error rate, a 30 percent failure rate in a 5 percent share adds only 1.5 percent. The analysis must compare the canary against the baseline version directly.

#### List the elements of a zero-downtime deployment on Kubernetes.

Correct probes, `maxUnavailable: 0` with a surge, a `preStop` delay with graceful shutdown and a sufficient grace period, a PodDisruptionBudget, multiple replicas, backward-compatible database and API changes, and a tested rollback.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Deployment installs code; release exposes behaviour. Good strategies separate the two.
- Rolling update advances on readiness only; blue-green gives instant rollback; canary limits exposure and needs per-version metrics and automation.
- A rollback of code never rolls back the database: use expand-contract so that old and new versions share the schema safely.
- In the simulation, detection time and traffic share at detection dominated the failed-request count (assumptions stated; not a measurement).
- Rehearse the rollback before it is needed.

A service that runs only on a developer laptop has no users. Running it for others requires machines that stay powered, networks that route traffic to them, a way to control who may change what, and a bill that matches the use. Amazon Web Services (AWS) is a public cloud: a catalogue of such building blocks rented by the hour or by the request. This chapter defines the vocabulary used by the rest of the Part (Region, Availability Zone, VPC, IAM) and treats identity and access management first, because every later step, from pushing an image to reading a database password, is an authorization decision.

Every AWS command shown in this Part was **not run on the build machine**: the build environment has no AWS account and no internet access. Command output is labelled `typical output (not run on the build machine)`. Service names, command syntax and policy format were checked against docs.aws.amazon.com and docs.github.com, consulted October 2026. Account identifiers such as `123456789012` and resource identifiers such as `subnet-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001` are placeholders.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Regions and Availability Zones

A **Region** is a geographic area that holds several isolated data-centre groups called **Availability Zones (AZs)**. `ap-south-1` (Mumbai) is the Region used in all examples. Resources are created inside one Region; most are not visible from another, which is the cause of the "resource not found" problems described later. An AZ failure is survivable only if the workload runs in at least two AZs, so production designs place two or more copies of each tier in different AZs.

blocks.text:
#### Shared responsibility and cost model

AWS operates the physical facilities and the hypervisor; the customer configures operating systems, networks rules, identities, data protection and application code. Billing is metered: instance hours, gigabytes stored, requests, data transferred out. Two consequences follow. A resource that is forgotten keeps billing, and a few services bill by the hour even when idle (per AWS pricing pages; exact rates change and are not quoted here). Per aws.amazon.com/free, consulted October 2026, a new account can start on a free plan that grants "$100 in credits immediately" and up to "$200 over 6 months" in total, and the plan ends "6 months after you open it or when your credits run out, whichever comes first"; 30+ services are "always free within monthly usage limits". These terms change, so the page must be re-read before opening an account.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Set a budget alert before creating any resource. A cost budget with an email alert (AWS Budgets, configured in the console) is the cheapest safeguard against an unexpected bill. Resources to delete after every exercise: EC2 instances, NAT gateways, load balancers, RDS instances and unattached Elastic IP addresses. Tagging every resource with `project=orders-lab` makes the final clean-up search reliable.

#### IAM: principals, policies, roles

**Identity and Access Management (IAM)** decides whether a request is allowed. A request is made by a **principal** (an IAM user, an IAM role session, or an AWS service) against a **resource** identified by an **Amazon Resource Name** **(ARN)** of the form `arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource`. Permissions are written as **policies**, JSON documents. Three kinds matter for this guide.

blocks.caption: IAM policy kinds used by the pipeline.

blocks.text:
A **role** has no password or permanent key. A trusted principal calls the Security Token Service (STS) and receives temporary credentials for the role. Temporary credentials are the basis of every secure pipeline: a long-lived access key (an access key id beginning `AKIA` plus a secret) can be copied, committed or leaked, whereas a role session expires.

Per docs.aws.amazon.com (policy grammar), a policy has an optional `Version`, a required `Statement`, and each statement needs `Effect` (`Allow` or `Deny`), `Action` and `Resource`. The grammar accepts `2008-10-17` and `2012-10-17`; the page does not say which to choose, but the examples in the ECS and GitHub documentation all use `2012-10-17`, which is the value used here. `Principal` is required in resource-based and trust policies and must not appear in identity-based policies.

The evaluation rules, per the policy evaluation logic page: an action allowed by an identity-based policy or a resource-based policy (same account) is allowed; an **explicit Deny in any applicable policy overrides every** **Allow**; permissions boundaries and Organizations service control policies (SCPs) restrict by intersection. A request matched by no Allow is denied (the implicit deny; the page implies it through the intersection rules and does not use the phrase).

blocks.text:
#### Least privilege

Least privilege means granting the minimum actions on the minimum resources for the minimum time. In practice: list actions explicitly rather than `ecs:*`; name resource ARNs rather than `"Resource": "*"`; use roles instead of users; add conditions such as `iam:PassedToService`. Some actions cannot be restricted to one resource; `ecr:GetAuthorizationToken` is the standard example and is granted on `*`.

### Worked example

The deployment pipeline of this Part needs one identity, the role `orders-ci-role`, which GitHub Actions assumes. Its identity policy allows pushing to one ECR repository and updating one ECS service. The action list for an ECR push is the set `ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability`, `ecr:InitiateLayerUpload`, `ecr:UploadLayerPart`, `ecr:CompleteLayerUpload` and `ecr:PutImage`, plus `ecr:GetAuthorizationToken` on `*` (this list was confirmed from memory of the ECR documentation, whose push page links to a separate permissions page; verify before use). The `iam:PassRole` statement is needed because registering a task definition names two roles, and passing a role to a service is itself a permission.

blocks.title: ci-policy.json

blocks.text: The trust policy of the same role states who may assume it. It names the GitHub OIDC provider as the federated principal and restricts the token subject to one repository and one GitHub environment. Per docs.github.com (OIDC in AWS), the provider URL is `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`, the audience is `sts.amazonaws.com`, and the page recommends restricting the `sub` claim; a `repo:owner/repo:*` pattern would admit every branch, pull request and environment of the repository.

blocks.title: trust-policy.json

blocks.text: Both files were parsed as JSON on the build machine. A small script can also review a policy before it is submitted. It cannot replace IAM Access Analyzer or the policy simulator, but it catches the commonest mistakes (wildcard actions, a `*` resource on an action that can be scoped).

$ python3 -I policycheck.py ci-policy.json trust-policy.json bad-policy.json

### Hands-on

1. Create an AWS account and, before anything else, create a budget with an email alert (console: Billing, Budgets).
2. Create an IAM role for a service (for example EC2) in the console and read the two policies it carries: the trust policy and the permissions policy.
3. In the console policy simulator, test `ecr:PutImage` against the repository ARN with `ci-policy.json` attached, then test `ecr:DeleteRepository`. The second request must be denied.
4. Run `policycheck.py` on a policy copied from a blog post. Every wildcard it reports is a statement to narrow.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### AccessDenied from an IAM role

**Scenario.** The deployment workflow assumes `orders-ci-role` and calls `aws ecs register-task-definition`. **Symptoms.** The step fails with `An error occurred (AccessDeniedException) when calling the` `RegisterTaskDefinition operation: User:` `arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/orders-ci-role/GitHubActions is not authorized to perform:` `iam:PassRole on resource: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/orders-task-role` (typical error text, not run). **Diagnosis.** The message names the principal, the missing action and the resource. The assumed-role ARN shows that the role was assumed correctly, so the trust policy is not the problem. **Root cause.** Registering a task definition that names a task role requires `iam:PassRole` on that role. The identity policy lacked it. **Fix.** Add the `PassTaskRolesToEcsOnly` statement shown above; keep the `iam:PassedToService` condition. **Prevention.** Test pipeline roles in the policy simulator before the first run, and read the error ARNs rather than widening the policy to `Action: "*"`.

A second variant: `Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` before any command runs. The cause is a trust policy whose `sub` condition does not equal the token claim. A job that declares `environment:` `production` produces the subject `repo:OWNER/REPO:environment:production`; a job without an environment on `main` produces `repo:OWNER/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main`. The condition must match the exact form.

#### Wrong Region

**Scenario.** A repository is created in `ap-south-1`, but a later command shows an empty list. **Symptoms.** `aws ecr` `describe-repositories` prints `"repositories": []`; the console shows nothing; the ECS service cannot find the image. **Diagnosis.** `aws configure get region` and the `--region` flag reveal the Region in use. The console shows the selected Region at the top right. **Root cause.** Regional resources are invisible from another Region; the CLI default Region differs from the console Region or from the workflow `AWS_REGION`. **Fix.** Pass `--region ap-south-1` explicitly or set `AWS_REGION` once in the workflow. **Prevention.** Declare one Region variable in the workflow and in the Terraform provider; never rely on a developer machine default.

#### Unexpected AWS bill

**Scenario.** A practice environment is left running for three weeks. **Symptoms.** A billing alert, or a statement showing charges for services nobody remembers using. **Diagnosis.** The Cost Explorer view grouped by service shows which resource type dominates; the tag filter `project=orders-lab` isolates the lab. **Root cause.** Typical sources are NAT gateways, load balancers, RDS instances that run continuously, idle EC2 instances, unattached public IPv4 addresses and large data transfer (from memory; verify current pricing). **Fix.** Delete the resources in reverse order of dependency (service, load balancer, database, NAT gateway, VPC), or delete the CloudFormation or Terraform stack that created them. **Prevention.** Budget alerts, resource tags, infrastructure as code (one command to destroy) and a calendar reminder for every lab.

### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?

A user has long-term credentials and belongs to one person or program. A role has no long-term credentials; a trusted principal assumes it and receives temporary credentials from STS. Pipelines and compute services should use roles.

#### What is the difference between a trust policy and a permissions policy?

The trust policy defines who may assume the role (the `Principal`). The permissions policy defines what the role may do after it is assumed. Both must be correct for a request to succeed.

#### How does AWS evaluate a request when several policies apply?

All applicable policies are evaluated. An explicit Deny wins. Otherwise an Allow is required from the identity-based or resource-based policy (and from every boundary or SCP that applies). With no Allow the request is denied.

#### Why is an AZ not the same as a Region?

A Region is a geographic area; an AZ is an isolated location inside it. High availability needs at least two AZs. Regional isolation is used for disaster recovery and data residency.

#### Why should pipelines use roles instead of access keys?

Keys are long-lived and are routinely leaked through repositories and logs. A role session is short-lived and is bound to a verified workload identity (see the OIDC section later in this Part).

**What does \`"Resource": "\*"\` on \`ecr:GetAuthorizationToken\` mean, and is it a violation of least**

#### privilege?

The action is not scoped to a repository, so `*` is the only valid resource. Least privilege is preserved by scoping the push actions to the repository ARN.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A Region is a geography; an AZ is an isolated failure domain inside it; subnets live in one AZ.
- IAM evaluates every request: an explicit Deny wins, otherwise an Allow is required.
- Roles with temporary credentials replace access keys; trust policies state who may assume them.
- Write least-privilege policies with explicit actions, resource ARNs and conditions, and review them before use.
- Set a budget alert first, tag everything and delete lab resources after use.

The container image of `orders-service` already runs under Docker Compose and Kubernetes (see the earlier Parts). Running it on AWS requires choosing a compute service, a network layout, a database, a way to supply secrets, a log destination and an entry point for traffic. This chapter explains each building block, then assembles them in the order in which they are created.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Compute options

rows: The instance, the operating system, Docker, patching, scaling
Learning, small fixed workloads, full control
Task definitions and services; AWS runs the hosts
Default choice for a small team running containers
Teams that already standardize on Kubernetes
Application bundle; the service builds the environment
Quick start for a jar; less transparent than ECS
blocks.caption: Choosing a compute service for a containerized Spring Boot service.

blocks.text:
**Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS)** is the AWS container scheduler. With the **Fargate** launch type no virtual machines are managed: each task is given dedicated CPU and memory. **Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS)** provides a managed Kubernetes control plane; the manifests of the previous chapters apply with AWS-specific ingress and storage classes. This guide uses ECS on Fargate, because it needs the fewest moving parts to reach production.

#### Network: VPC, subnets, gateways

A **Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)** is a private network with an address range such as `10.0.0.0/16`. Per docs.aws.amazon.com (VPC), a subnet is an address range inside the VPC and resides in one AZ; a subnet is **public** when its route table sends internet-bound traffic to an **internet gateway**, and **private** when it does not. Instances in a private subnet reach the internet through a **NAT gateway**, which sits in a public subnet and permits outbound connections only. A **security group** is a stateful firewall attached to a network interface; a network ACL is a stateless filter attached to a subnet (stateful and stateless as general AWS behaviour, not stated on the page consulted).

blocks.text:
#### The ECS object model

A **task definition** is a versioned blueprint (image, CPU, memory, ports, environment, secrets, log configuration). A **task** is one running instance of it. A **service** keeps a desired number of tasks running, replaces failed ones and performs rolling deployments. A **cluster** is the logical group. Two roles appear, and confusing them is a frequent cause of failures: the **task execution role** is used by the ECS agent to pull the image, write logs and fetch secrets before the container starts; the **task role** is used by the application code to call AWS APIs.

blocks.text:
Per docs.aws.amazon.com (task definition parameters), Fargate requires `networkMode awsvpc` and task-level `cpu` and `memory` from a fixed set of combinations; for example 256 CPU units allow 512, 1024 or 2048 MiB, and 1024 units allow 2048 to 8192 MiB. `essential` defaults to true: if an essential container stops, the whole task stops.

#### Load balancing and health checks

An **Application Load Balancer (ALB)** terminates HTTP and HTTPS and forwards requests to a **target group**. For Fargate (awsvpc) the target group must use target type `ip`. The ALB probes each target. Per docs.aws.amazon.com (target group health checks): the defaults are protocol HTTP, path `/`, interval 30 seconds, timeout 5 seconds (the CLI reference lists 6 for HTTP), healthy threshold 5, unhealthy threshold 2 and success code 200. A target that fails the unhealthy threshold of consecutive checks is taken out of service; if every target is unhealthy the ALB routes to all of them regardless ("fail-open"). For `orders-service` the path must be `/actuator/health`, and the service needs a **health check grace period** so that the ECS scheduler does not kill a task that is still starting the JVM.

blocks.text:
#### Data, secrets, logs, DNS and certificates

**Amazon RDS** runs PostgreSQL as a managed instance. The instance belongs to a **DB subnet group** that spans at least two AZs (per the RDS documentation) and, for this design, is not publicly accessible; its security group allows port 5432 only from the application security group. **AWS Secrets Manager** stores the database password; with `--manage-master-user-password` RDS creates and manages the master password in Secrets Manager (per the `create-db-instance` reference). **Systems Manager Parameter Store** holds non-secret and low-sensitivity configuration. **Amazon S3** stores objects such as exports and static assets. **CloudWatch Logs** receives container output through the `awslogs` log driver; **CloudWatch alarms** evaluate metrics such as `HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count`. **Route 53** maps a domain name to the load balancer and **AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)** issues the TLS certificate that the ALB listener uses; both are configured at the level of a DNS record and a certificate ARN in this guide.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Secrets are injected when the task starts. Per docs.aws.amazon.com (ECS secrets), a secret referenced in `secrets.valueFrom` is resolved when the container starts. A rotated secret is not delivered to running containers; a new deployment (`--force-new-deployment`) is required. The task execution role needs `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`, and `kms:Decrypt` when a customer managed key is used. In a private subnet an interface VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager (or a NAT gateway) is required.
